80.t: How the plunger and bucket mutes began
80.s: Players tried toilet plungers and tin cans in Harlem clubs, and a manufacturer copied the ideas and sold them back.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: Naw. No, that I don't know. I tell you why, because I think it was Frankie's idea. I'm almost positive it was. But later on, at that time I can tell you because we had a lot of musicians, a lot of everybody used to come in Small's, come to Harlem to see and dig the musicians, and then what are you…

80.t: Felt-hat mutes and other improvised mutes
80.s: He explains how derby hats and tin hats were cut and softened into personal mutes, and that players also used water glasses and cuspidors to find a distinctive sound.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: The felt hat, the derby hat, that all ties in, because we used a derby, people throw derbies away, you know, they take them away until they turn. They buy a black derby and wear it until it turns green. You know.

80.t: Claiming the muted-trumpet style before Jonah Jones
80.s: He says he used the mute long before Jonah, going back to Dyer Jones and Fats, while Jonah was told to use mutes at the Embers.
80.q: And with the show, in fact before Fats I was using the mute, you know, when I first met Dolly, and Dyer Jones, and all that business with the shows, and the carnivals, and all that stuff.

80.t: Being noted for his mute at the Embers; two years in and out
80.s: By the Embers years he was established for his mute and liked its crisp, stinging sound, working there off and on for about two years.
80.q: No I had my mutes (Inaudible) because I was -- this is after -- well, this is much after Fats. I mean I had been established, because I'm noted for my mute, you know? And I like it. I like the mute. I like the -- I like that crisp and stinging sound, you know, effect that the mute can give with me…

80.t: Dyer Jones teaches him the Harmon mute and plunger
80.s: She showed him the wah-wah Harmon mute and plunger during the show, and he drove his hotel neighbours crazy practising.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: Everything was so nice. And I'm sitting there trying to learn -- this is my well, second or third day in show business, maybe the second week, and I'm trying to learn, hoping to be good someday, and this woman sat there, and she was out of this world. So finally she turned to me, and she said,…

80.t: Challenging Dyer later; learning the mutes; credit on Fats Waller records
80.s: He later teased Dyer, learned the wah-wah in a week, and believes his muted playing behind Fats Waller on Victor drew credit that really came from her.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: I think Dyer passed some time -- I'm almost positive that she passed some time ago, but what a trumpeter, you know, what a trumpet player she was. And she and I were pals there for quite some time. So I used to kid her, after I met her that time I came back years later. I said "Remember? Remember…

80.t: Frankie Newton and the buzz mute at Small's Paradise
80.s: Meeting Frankie Newton in Charlie Johnson's band, he got Newton's buzz mute, which had passed through Johnny Hamilton.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: Buzz? Ah, that's another story. A good friend of mine, Frankie Newton, in New York, I was working at Charlie Johnson's band down at Small's Paradise, and that's where I first met him. Frankie Newton, one of the greatest trumpet players in the world, I still say, and he has a lot of fans who think…

418.t: Frankie Newton and his homemade mute
418.s: He played with Frankie Newton before Heywood, and recalls Newton's homemade vice mute full of holes.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: Yeah, well he made it his self. It had a lot of holes and things in it. I don't know what he had inside of it. He might have had some dollar bills in there rattling.

418.t: Frankie Newton and his homemade mute
418.s: He played with Frankie Newton before Heywood, and recalls Newton's homemade mute full of holes.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: Yeah. Well, he made it himself, you know. It had a whole lot of holes and things in it. I don't know what he had inside of it. He might have had some dollar bills in there rattling.

418.t: Frankie Newton and his homemade mute
418.s: He played with Frankie Newton before Heywood, and recalls Newton's homemade mute full of holes.
418.ch: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
418.q: Yeah, well he made it his self. It had a lot of holes and things in it. I don't know what he had inside of it. He might have had some dollar bills in there rattling.

241.s: He has long used plungers, coffee cans, milk cans and a glass over the bell to vary the trumpet sound.
241.q: Well, I just, well, Mr. Bill, I just, sometime I, I've been doing that, you know, sometime I used to use that rubber spludger. Yeah, plunger. I used to use that long time ago. Then sometime I used to take a coffee can, you know what I mean? I'd make a, take a coffee can. I'd take that coffee can…

241.t: The derby mute and the kettle mute
241.s: He made a derby mute holder from a coat hanger, got a derby by mail, gave one up to a visiting musician, and made a kettle-pot mute for Nelson.
241.q: That's right. That's what they had, you see? So, and everybody seen with that thing, man, say, why ain't the derby got that pot from, it's called a pot, you know what I mean? Yeah. I said, where you got that thing from? I said, man, I sent off and got that.

689.t: Joe Oliver's mutes, plunger and derby demonstration
689.s: Dominique and Russell handle mutes on the table: long silver, con mute, plunger, tin can and derby hat effects Oliver used.
689.q: Yeah. He used that quite a bit. Because it was easier to blow than this short mute here. You see? The short mute here. It's kind of a strainer. He used a short mute like this. A con mute. Yeah.

689.t: Manuel Perez's mute use, plunger origins and the coconut shell
689.s: Perez used mutes on waltzes; the plunger was a Chicago-era thing like the tin can, and Dominique never saw a coconut shell used.
689.q: Worked up here. See that plunger? Same thing as taking a can. Yeah. Same thing. They do that with the tin can? Tin can. We used to do it with the tin can.

256.t: Plungers, derbies, cans and other mute effects
256.s: Plunger on Lonesome Road, hats, molasses cans in New Orleans, Dave Kline's bulb, phonograph record in the bell.
256.q: Oh, yeah, yeah. I used a plunger on a record. I think it was Muggsy's Lonesome Road. People wrote in the crystal. What is that instrument on there? They didn't know it was a trombone. It was on Lonesome Road. And then Muggsy and I used to do a lot with Ted Lewis, and then we'd take the hats with…

256.s: Lewis featured him on rhythm with the first wow-wow mute, made by Patty Harmon.
256.q: I used to sit down front. I used to use the first wow-wow mute ever made that Patty Harmon made. And he'd say, play me rhythm, Brunus. Give me rhythm. And I'd just have to hold the thing choked and pump out rhythm.

306.t: Rene's birth record, his father, and Buddy Petit's wah-wah mute
306.s: Rene checks his baptismal record, remembers his guitarist father, and credits Buddy Petit's derby with leading him to invent the wah-wah.
306.ch: Joe Rene: Lewis, the Rena band and New Orleans
306.q: So I went down to the Catholic Church. I was born to the Catholic Church. I went down there, and I got my boy's sister, and I was surprised. And I always owned the impression that I was born with Marshall Levin, or the first. But when I look on that verse, it was Marshall Levin. Marshall Levin. Mm.…

306.t: Mutes: coconut shell, derby and plunger, and rock and roll
306.s: Rene tells how mute ideas came from Buddy Petit's derby, a coconut shell and a plunger used by Chris Kelly, and ends by arguing jazz will outlast rock and roll.
306.ch: Brother's trumpet and the early players
306.q: of course, they didn't want to give me the credit. I didn't want it, no, huh? Because all I was trying to do, take the ideas, you know, to get ahead of the other fella. I went to the, this must have been back in 1910 or 11, but way back then, got a coconut shell and cut it in half. Because you see,…

106.t: Johnny Dunn and the cup mute origin story
106.s: Briggs says Johnny Dunn imitated Keppard but told him he discovered the effect himself with a cup; they worked together at the Sporting Club in Monte Carlo.
106.ch: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
106.q: He got that himself -- he probably did. The idea, or something happened. Johnny told me himself, because for a short time we worked together at the Sportin' in Monte Carlo.

106.t: Coconut shells, plungers and Joe Oliver's fist
106.s: Discussion of early mutes: Smith and others used coconut shells, Dunn and Bubber Miley claimed the wah-wah, and Oliver used his fist in the bell.
106.ch: Paris, the Blackbirds and Noble Sissle
106.q: I don't know, 'cause I was in Europe, you see. I believe that it came in later, because Johnny Dunn, as I mentioned to you, he said he had found that wah-wah thing, but to me --

687.s: He seldom uses a mute himself but used straight and cup mutes with Duke; he used a plunger when younger, as Sidney still does.
687.q: in my own personal playing I seldom use a mute but in a lot of the things that I had to do in Duke's band I did use mutes

245.s: He used wah-wah mutes, kazoos, a plunger and cans.
245.q: oh yeah i had wah wah mutes and i had all kinds of mutes and i had one of those uh could you know those folk kuzooks oh yeah i couldn't vote four of them together and made a mute out that like jazz mutes see and i use a a plunger one of those toilet plunges you know and make it go wow wow like that…

246.t: Low trumpet playing, wah-wah rubber and coconut mutes
246.s: Glass describes homemade mutes of plumber's rubber and coconut shell, and says Buddy and Chris Kelly believed in the derby.
246.q: Him and Lil' Keg and Bob would get together, you had a good line. What about getting that low on trumpet, you know, like Toka does? Many of the other ones do that? Yeah. You know, hit them pedal notes like he does? Yeah, the D. Yeah, the D. The D would play real low then? Yeah, the D can get all…

955.t: Perez versus Wooden Joe, and trumpet mutes
955.s: He compares Perez's leading with Wooden Joe's hardness and variation, then describes coconut-shell and plunger mutes.
955.q: Well, in the later days he switched the trumpet. But when I first met him, he was playing one of those cornet, E-flat cornet.

33.t: Mutes and the cup mute he invented in 1917
33.s: DeDroit describes fiber straight mutes and how he made a cup mute from a Salisbury cigarette can in 1917 without copyrighting it.
33.ch: Other bands, mutes, arrangers and composers
33.q: Yeah. There was a, Mr. Peterson who was the dean of all the drummers, he taught all the drummers, his name was George Peterson, he used to make them out of fiber. Out of what? Fiber, some kind of fiber. Red. Fiber? Oh, I call it fiber. It's a stiff material. It's a cardboard. And I invented a lot…

183.t: Mutes: derby, felt and metal, and not having one as a boy
183.s: They discuss mutes, with Watts saying he had none as a child and that a felt derby gives a better tone than a metal one.
183.ch: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
183.q: No, the real derby gives you a better effect. The real, better effect. I had both since I was doing my musical career. Yeah, you had the ten derby. I had both of them, but that old.

752.t: Oliver's mutes, kazoo and derby effects
752.s: Mutes Oliver used, the one he gave Mugsy, and kazoo, glass and derby effects.
752.q: He had a kazooke, a big kazooke. He tied two of them together and had a blow and hold that kazooke. You know the kazooke where they blew the blow? Yes.

274.t: Use of mutes among local players
274.s: They discuss mute use by trumpet and trombone players and Sam Morgan's skill with mutes.
274.q: You know one used to use horn mute? Sam Horgan. I never seen a man use mutes like Sam Horgan. He knew what to do with them though. Sam had a good plan.

187.t: The cup mute fill-ins with Kid Thomas
187.s: His accompaniment with a cup device that Thomas brought, which he plays to fill in.
187.q: It just came to me since Thomas gave me that cup. I never did use nothing like that. Thomas brought that there. I just fill in, that's all.

45.s: They discuss how trumpeters held and used the derby mute and the origin of the wah-wah effect.
45.q: They'd just hold it. Sometimes they'd put it on the top, but sometimes they'd just hold it on the side. You've seen Sharky Heights.

923.t: Tom as the first to mute a horn, and Ted 'Steve' Brown
923.s: Mrs. Brown says Tom was first to mute a horn, making a tin mute, and Teagarden offered a mouthpiece for it; Ted is called Steve.
923.ch: New Orleans bands and later photographs
923.q: And he made it in his shop out of tin. And he said when he went to Chicago, they couldn't understand the weird tones. So Teagarden, I says, gave him, oh, a beautiful mouthpiece. If he'd give him that mute. Could Tom...

285.t: Props, the kazoo mute and the kazoo craze
285.s: He used props like a tin barrel and derbies, and invented a kazoo mute for his horn that others copied.
285.q: And so we used to open up this thing and I used to wave that hat, you know, and people kept saying, what's going on? Some lady in Boston interviewed me one time. I think she was with the Boston Travelers, a musical critic. And she came backstage, we were playing in Boston. And I used to have…

8.t: Oliver's mutes: derby, glass and tin can
8.s: Oliver and Keppard used derbies, glasses and tin cans as mutes; there was no name for such players.
8.q: Joe used to use a derby used to use a big old tin can like the apples or something coming in and five gallons not five or two gallons can you know blowing it you know Freddie Keppard used to teach his derby too you know mm-hmm

55.s: Trumpet players adopting the little cup mute after Bolden.
55.q: All the trumpet players start to carry a look. And little little. Little dinner cups like. Oh yes. I know what you mean. Sure. I know what you mean. Sure. I know. I know. I know. I know. Sure.

483.s: Chris made the horn speak using a plunger and his derby hat, the first mute man Kelly knew.
483.q: Yeah. But I mean, he did make it a different thing. But I mean, he could say his name with a trumpet with his hand. Was that it? Yeah. He was the first mute man I knew in that field. You know, to say something, you know, like a guy who worked a trumpet and bring out an expression. Well, he was the…

270.t: Growl trumpet and mutes: derby, glass and bottle; Chris Kelly
270.s: Cootie growled by hand, derby or glass; Sayles and a trumpeter visitor swap talk of aluminium mutes, Chris Kelly's blues on a derby, and improvised mutes.
270.q: well he played open horn but like I say in playing that that growl you did it with your hand or you did it with a derby or you did it with a glass and he was very good at it and the New Orleans boys did that too oh sure they once and I don't remember where it started down the way else did it but…

198.t: Using a derby or bucket as a mute
198.s: Without a derby, players used buckets or cans as mutes; the tone was deeper than a sax.
198.q: Well, if you didn't have a derby, we could use anything you could get your hand on, like a bucket or a can or something like that, you know? Or even if they had a luminal derby there, we'd use that. Sometimes it's feeling good, except I don't know. Hello? Aubrey, go outside.

58.t: Mutes: cola bottle, straight mute and Harmon
58.s: Punch recalls cola bottle mutes in New Orleans, the buzz mute, and the later Harmon mute he saw in Chicago.
58.q: you know yeah you take a cola bottle and put it in that bar and make it sound good yeah he the freshman started that and i come here they were doing that eating a cola bottle and they used to didn't have no cup like that just had straight and they started to make them straight like that then they…

997.t: Mutt Carey and the eggshell mute; replacing Zutty at the Elite
997.s: He worked with Mutt Carey, who used half an eggshell in his horn, and took over from Zutty Singleton.
997.q: Yeah, egg shell and blow it out you know. That's facts. I've seen him do that. I feel like.

443.s: He demonstrates open horn, Harmon, plunger and cup mutes and what each does.
443.q: Well the mutes, okay, I love working with mutes because it can change the texture of what you’re playing. All right open horn. [audio] Make it ring, all right, okay. So then you take a Harmon mute and you take the stem out and you get close to the microphone and you approximately what Miles [audio]…

60.t: His patched Olds cornet and cup mutes
60.s: Description of the 1930s Olds cornet, button mute and improvised cups.
60.q: It’s a cornet. There’s bubble gum covering here — well not bubble gum just regular gum — and with some masking tape on until I get it fixed. But I’ve got patches on it all over. It’s early 30s, it’s an Olds, a Los Angeles Olds and it’s early 30s. I got it for $75 and I wasn’t interested in the horn…

108.t: 'No Greater Love' and the plunger mute
108.s: They listen to his recording of 'No Greater Love', which sounds like two trumpeters, and he explains he used a plunger as a Harmon-like mute.
108.q: That’s exactly what I had in mind, too. It’s like a put on but you know, you’re kidding with yourself, like it’s two different guys.

101.t: The Harmon mute with stem removed
101.s: Terry says St. Louis players took the stem out before Miles did.
101.q: There was a time in St. Louis that all the trumpet players – I don’t know actually who really started it. A lot of people think Miles started it, but he didn’t. Cats were doing that in St. Louis long before Miles played a Harmon. They would take the stems out of the mute and play, because a lot of…

367.t: Developing his cup mute and plunger sound; Clark Terry
367.s: Young says he used the cup mute to sound different from open-horn players like Sweets and Joe Newman, and praises Clark Terry's own sound.
367.q: That‘s a good question, too. I started, I don‘t know why I started doing that. I started doing that because I wanted to sound different than some of the other trumpet players in the band and I got used to playing with the, there was a cup mute, sometimes I used a plunger. But then I switched from…

67.t: Musicians guarding their ideas: Elmer Snowden and Jack Hatton
67.s: Players removed tune titles, reversed banjo strings and played with their backs turned; Jack Hatton used buckets and bottles before mutes existed.
67.q: Well, you know, the musicians -- some of them in those days, they wanted to be -- they had a feeling that you were going to steal something from them. Or take something from them.

70.t: Playing the plunger: Tricky Sam's ya-ya versus Tyree's wa
70.s: Jackson copied Tricky Sam's plunger sound, relaxing it, getting closer to the ya-ya than Tyree Glenn.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: So when I joined the band and I started to playing the plunger, all I did was take Tricky Sam's style, actually, and relax it, you know, and try to bring it up to, you know, make it a little, you know, more relaxed.

71.t: Playing louder after Basie and 'Cup Mute Clayton'
71.s: He says he played strongly before and after Basie, who kept him muted, and wrote 'Cup Mute Clayton' ironically.
71.ch: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
71.q: And as soon as I got away from Basie, I played that way again in the Army. Strong. Still in California, I never touched a mute unless it was just for something special. Joined Basie and played the mute. When I left and went into the Army I played like I wanted, loud naturally. So I played the same…

124.t: Mutes, matching sounds, and Stan Kenton's Ellington imitation
124.s: Brass sections cut mute corks to match; Kenton tried for Ellington's sound but Duke's plunger effects confused white musicians.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: If they're going to use a harmon mute, they cut the rubbers down -- the thing on the mute so they can get the mute in further --

473.t: The bucket mute, the "Jonah Jones mute" and playing open again
473.s: He varied mutes (growl, plunger, hummer), the bucket mute got his name in the studios without payment, and with Cozy Cole he now plays open more than in the Embers days.
473.ch: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
473.q: So I used the growl, plunger, and the hummer and different things. And in the studio they was calling them mutes the Jonah Jones mutes, that bucket mute. You know, I didn't get a penny out of that, because I know they was telling me, 'Well, I hope you're getting your bread out of here, because when…
